prompt: `pg_column_size(embedding)` printed `1544` for a `vector(384)`. The 384 numbers take 1,536 bytes. What are the other 8?
hint: The section says what the extra bytes hold.

choices.text: The article's id, stored inside the value
choices.why: The id is its own column, `id text`. The vector value holds numbers and a little bookkeeping about them, nothing from other columns.

choices.text: A pgvector header holding size and dimension
choices.why: Right. Every vector value carries a short header of 8 bytes beside its 4 × d bytes of float32.

choices.text: Two extra float64 coordinates added by Python
choices.why: psycopg sends what `register_vector` encodes, and pgvector stores every coordinate as float32; nothing adds coordinates, and `vector_dims` printed 384.

choices.text: The row header and pointer PostgreSQL adds in front of every row it stores
choices.why: That overhead is real but belongs to the row, which lesson 18 weighs. `pg_column_size` measured only this one value.

prompt: A model returns 768 dimensions and the column is `vector(768)` in pgvector 0.6.0. What does `pg_column_size` report for one stored vector?
hint: Four bytes a number, plus the header the section measured.

prompt: The `articles` table was filled with all-MiniLM-L6-v2. A later script stores one article's vector from a different model that also returns 384 numbers. What does PostgreSQL do?
hint: What exactly does `vector(384)` check?

choices.text: Refuses it with `expected 384 dimensions`
choices.why: That error needs a different length. Both models return 384 numbers, so the length check passes.

choices.text: Refuses it, because pgvector records which model wrote the column
choices.why: pgvector stores numbers and a dimension. Nothing in the type names a model, which is why the section says to put the model's name in the schema yourself.

choices.text: Stores it with no error and no warning at all
choices.why: Right. Only the length is checked, and a vector from another model of the same dimension is meaningless beside the others while looking exactly like them.

choices.text: Stores it and normalises it to the column's other vectors
choices.why: No conversion happens. pgvector keeps the numbers it receives, and no arithmetic maps one model's space onto another's.

prompt: To find out which pgvector a PostgreSQL you did not install is running, read the ___ column of `pg_extension` for `vector`.
hint: The lab's answer was 0.6.0.

prompt: A larger inner product means more similar, yet `ORDER BY embedding <#> q` puts the most similar row first. Why?
hint: Look at the sign in the last column of `ops.sql`.

choices.text: PostgreSQL sorts descending when the operator is `<#>`
choices.why: `ORDER BY` without `DESC` is ascending for every operator; nothing special happens for this one.

choices.text: `<#>` is the cosine distance under another name
choices.why: `<=>` is the cosine distance. `<#>` printed `-0.44556307792663574` for h18, a negative number, which no distance is.

choices.text: It returns that number with its sign flipped
choices.why: Right. Flipping the sign makes smaller mean closer, the order an index scan walks, so the same ascending sort works for all three operators.

choices.text: The vectors are stored negated when `register_vector` sends them
choices.why: The vectors arrive as the model made them; the length column printed 1.0000 and `<=>` gave ordinary positive distances.

prompt: Two vectors of length 1 have a cosine distance, `<=>`, of 0.25. What does `<#>` return for the same pair?
hint: The section relates the negative inner product to the cosine distance.

prompt: `recall.sql` returned five rows for the 24 test questions. What do the five rows tell you?
hint: Read the outer `WHERE`.

choices.text: Five questions put an article outside their relevant list first, so 19 of 24 were right at rank 1
choices.why: Right. The lateral search finds each question's first article, and the `WHERE` keeps only the misses.

choices.text: Five questions have no relevant article in the table
choices.why: Every row shows a `relevant` list, and the articles named in it are in `articles`; the miss is in the ranking.

choices.text: The `LATERAL` join stops after five questions
choices.why: It ran for all 24. The `LIMIT 1` is inside the subquery and limits each question's search to one article.

choices.text: Five articles were never returned for any question
choices.why: The query lists questions, not articles, and h09 appears twice among the five rows.

prompt: Put in order what happens when `search.py` answers one question.
hint: Two steps happen in Python, three in PostgreSQL, and one in Python again.
items: Send the vector as a query parameter
Compute `<=>` between it and every row's vector
Sort the rows by that distance, smallest first
Print one minus each distance as the similarity
trap: The vectors of the articles never travel to Python: the distance and the sort both happen inside PostgreSQL, and only three rows come back.

prompt: After `CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw` on the 40 articles, `EXPLAIN` still shows `Seq Scan on articles`. Why?
hint: Who chooses the plan, and on what grounds?

choices.text: The index is still being built in the background
choices.why: `CREATE INDEX` had returned before `EXPLAIN` ran; the index was complete and ready.

choices.text: HNSW indexes need `SET enable_seqscan = off` before the planner will consider them
choices.why: On the 20,000-row table the same kind of index was used with no setting changed.

choices.text: The planner estimated that reading 40 rows costs less than walking the graph
choices.why: Right. The planner picks the cheapest plan it can estimate, and a table that fits in a few pages is cheapest to read whole.

choices.text: The query used `<=>`, and the index was built for `<->`
choices.why: The index was built with `vector_cosine_ops`, which is the class for `<=>`; the operator matched.

prompt: An index was built `USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)`. Which of these queries is the planner able to answer with it?
hint: Operator, direction and a `LIMIT`.

choices.text: `ORDER BY 1 - (embedding <=> q) DESC LIMIT 5`
choices.why: The same order on paper, but the planner does not do the algebra; `unused.sql` got a `Seq Scan` for exactly this.

choices.text: `ORDER BY embedding <=> q LIMIT 5`
choices.why: Right. Column, the operator the class names, the value, ascending, and a limit: the one shape the index serves.

choices.text: `ORDER BY embedding <-> q LIMIT 5`
choices.why: `<->` is the L2 distance, served by `vector_l2_ops`. `unused.sql` showed the cosine index ignored for it.

choices.text: `ORDER BY embedding <=> q DESC LIMIT 5`
choices.why: Descending asks for the farthest rows first, which is not what the index walks towards.

prompt: With an IVFFlat index of `lists = 100` on the 40 articles, `search.py` printed one row instead of three. What explains it?
hint: Two numbers: how many groups exist and how many a query visits.

choices.text: IVFFlat returns only the nearest row whatever the `LIMIT`
choices.why: On a table big enough for its groups, an IVFFlat scan fills the `LIMIT`; the one row came from this index's state, not from the method.

choices.text: The HNSW index on the same column conflicted with it
choices.why: Two indexes on one column do not interfere. The planner picked one, the IVFFlat, and its answer was short.

choices.text: The query searched one group of a hundred, and it held one article
choices.why: Right. `ivfflat.probes` was 1, and a hundred groups learnt from 40 rows leave each one nearly empty.

choices.text: The NOTICE aborted half of the index build
choices.why: The `NOTICE` was a warning and `CREATE INDEX` completed; the index held every row, in groups the query mostly did not visit.

prompt: Match each operator to the operator class an index needs for it to be used.
hint: The class names the distance.

prompt: An IVFFlat scan looks in as many of its groups as the setting `ivfflat.___` says, and pgvector 0.6.0 sets it to 1 unless you change it.
hint: The section showed it with `SHOW`.

prompt: Without an index, the plan for the `noise` search showed `Parallel Seq Scan ... rows=6667 loops=3`. About how many rows were read in total?
hint: `rows` is per loop, and there were three loops.

prompt: Why does Supabase's guide put the vector search inside a SQL function and call it with `rpc`?
hint: What does a Supabase client send?

choices.text: pgvector on Supabase works only inside functions
choices.why: The column, the operators and the indexes work in any SQL there. The function exists for the client's sake.

choices.text: The generated API has no way to order by a pgvector operator
choices.why: Right. The client talks to an API that filters and sorts by columns, and a function called through it runs the SQL the API cannot express.

choices.text: Functions run faster, because PostgreSQL caches the vectors they have already read
choices.why: Nothing is cached by the function. `LANGUAGE sql STABLE` lets the planner treat it like the query inside it, which is the same speed.

choices.text: So the embedding model runs on Supabase's servers
choices.why: The function takes a vector already computed. The program embeds the question on the caller's side, with the same model as the articles.

prompt: A team declares its search function `SECURITY DEFINER`, owned by an administrator, so that it 'always works'. The `articles` table has a row-level security policy per shop. What has changed?
hint: Whose rights does the function run with now?

choices.text: Nothing, because policies are checked on the table whoever runs the query
choices.why: Policies apply to the role running the query, and a `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs as its owner, whose role the policy may not restrict.

choices.text: The function now refuses every call from the browser
choices.why: Definer rights widen what the function reads; they do not stop anybody from calling it.

choices.text: Only the speed: definer functions skip the planner
choices.why: The planner runs either way. What changes is whose policies apply.

choices.text: Any caller searches every shop's articles through it
choices.why: Right. The function runs with its owner's rights and skips the caller's policies, so the search became a way round them.

prompt: `match_articles` declares its parameter as `vector(384)`. A caller passes a vector of 256 numbers. What happens?
hint: The section ran exactly this.

choices.text: The call is refused with `expected 384 dimensions, not 256`
choices.why: That is the column's error on an INSERT. A function's parameter size is ignored, so the vector gets in.

choices.text: It gets in, and `<=>` fails with `different vector dimensions 384 and 256`
choices.why: Right. PostgreSQL ignores the size written on a parameter, and the operator refuses to compare vectors of different lengths.

choices.text: It is padded with zeros to 384 and scored
choices.why: Nothing pads a vector. The `matchdims` capture ended in an error, with no rows.

choices.text: The function returns zero rows, because nothing passes the threshold
choices.why: No row was scored at all; the comparison itself failed.

prompt: In `$vectorSearch`, `numCandidates` plays the part of which pgvector setting?
hint: Both decide how wide an approximate search looks before it keeps the best.

choices.text: `hnsw.ef_search`
choices.why: Right. Both size the list of candidates an HNSW-style search gathers; Atlas takes it in every query, pgvector as a session setting.

choices.text: The `LIMIT` of the query
choices.why: `limit` has its own field in `$vectorSearch`, and `numCandidates` cannot be smaller than it.

choices.text: The `lists` given at `CREATE INDEX`
choices.why: `lists` is fixed when an IVFFlat index is built. `numCandidates` changes per query.

choices.text: The dimension in `vector(384)`
choices.why: The dimension is `numDimensions` in Atlas's index definition, not a field of the query.

prompt: A team moves its search from pgvector to Atlas, with a `cosine` index, and keeps its rule 'drop results under 0.4', tuned on `1 - (a <=> b)`. What happens to the results?
hint: Atlas's score is (1 + cosine) / 2.

choices.text: Nothing changes; a cosine is a cosine
choices.why: Atlas does not return the cosine. Its score is rescaled to run from 0 to 1.

choices.text: Almost nothing passes, because Atlas scores run lower
choices.why: The rescaling moves scores up for every cosine below 1, so the threshold lets more through, not less.

choices.text: Far more passes, since 0.4 there is only a cosine of −0.2
choices.why: Right. (1 + c) / 2 = 0.4 gives c = −0.2, so results that pgvector would have dropped as unrelated now pass.

choices.text: The query fails until the threshold is given as a distance
choices.why: `$vectorSearch` has no threshold field at all; the rule is the team's own code, and it runs on whatever score comes back.

prompt: In MongoDB Atlas the vector search is a stage of an aggregation pipeline, called ___, and it has to be the pipeline's first stage.
hint: Its name starts with a dollar sign.

prompt: `edit.py` updated the refund article's body, then tried to store a WordLlama vector in the same transaction. What did the article's body read afterwards?
hint: The second line of the output.

choices.text: The new text, with the old vector beside it
choices.why: That is what two systems would leave. Here both updates were in one transaction, and the error rolled back both.

choices.text: The old text, as if the script had never run
choices.why: Right. The vector was refused, PostgreSQL rolled back the whole transaction, and the body still said three working days.

choices.text: Nothing; the row was deleted by the failed update
choices.why: A failed `UPDATE` does not delete. The fresh connection read the row back.

choices.text: The new text with a vector truncated to 256 numbers
choices.why: pgvector does not truncate; it refused the value with `expected 384 dimensions, not 256`.

prompt: A team checks that its search uses the HNSW index by running `EXPLAIN` against a staging copy of 300 rows, and sees `Seq Scan`. Production has two million rows. What should they conclude?
hint: Which plan the planner picks depends on what it estimates.

choices.text: The index is broken and must be rebuilt
choices.why: A `Seq Scan` on a small table is the planner's correct choice, as it was on the 40 articles; it says nothing about the index's health.

choices.text: Nothing about production; the plan has to be checked on a table of production's size
choices.why: Right. The choice follows the table's size, so a small copy is answered with a full read whatever the index.

choices.text: Production will also read every row, since a plan does not change with the table's size
choices.why: It does change: the same query on 20,000 rows of `noise` switched to an `Index Scan`.

choices.text: The operator class is wrong for the query
choices.why: A wrong class gives a `Seq Scan` at every size, which is why it is checked on the large table; a 300-row result alone cannot tell the two apart.

prompt: Marginalia keeps its help-centre vectors in a column of the PostgreSQL that holds its orders. Which of these does it get without building anything more? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about what the rest of the data already has.

choices.text: A text and its vector saved or rolled back together
choices.why: Yes. Both are in one row and one transaction, as `edit.py` showed.

choices.text: Vectors in the same backups as the texts
choices.why: Yes. `pg_dump` and every other backup of the database include the column.

choices.text: A guarantee that a `LIMIT 10` search through the index always returns 10 rows
choices.why: An approximate index can return fewer rows, as the IVFFlat did here and as lesson 16 shows for HNSW.

choices.text: Joins between search results and the other tables, in one statement
choices.why: Yes. `recall.sql` joined the questions to the articles; orders or stock join the same way.

choices.text: A check that every vector came from the same model
choices.why: The column checks only the dimension. Two models of 384 dimensions pass it alike.

prompt: Put in order the steps for adding IVFFlat search to an existing PostgreSQL database.
hint: One index type learns from the rows that exist when it is built.
items: Add a table or column of type `vector(384)`
`EXPLAIN` the search on the full table
trap: The index comes after the load: IVFFlat learns its groups from the rows present at `CREATE INDEX`, and on the 40 articles it printed a `NOTICE` and lost rows. HNSW could have been created earlier.
